cards.front: What three things do binding proteins control in order to route a signal?
cards.back: Which partners meet, where they meet, and when they can act.
cards.quote: Binding proteins route signals by controlling which partners meet, where they meet, and when they can act.

cards.front: Name three limits on the idea that binding proteins route signals (adaptors, docking proteins, scaffolds).
cards.back: Binding alone may not activate a pathway; not every scaffold lacks enzyme activity; more scaffold does not always mean more signal.
cards.quote: Binding alone may not activate a pathway, not every scaffold lacks enzyme activity, and more scaffold does not always mean more signal.

cards.front: An {{c1::adaptor}} has no enzyme activity and supplies a link between partners.
cards.back: Grb2 is the model.
cards.quote: An adaptor has no enzyme activity and supplies a link between partners.
cards.section: Three ways to organize a signal

cards.front: A docking protein is itself phosphorylated at several sites and supplies a {{c1::regulated platform}} for several partners.
cards.back: IRS-1 is the model.
cards.quote: A docking protein is itself phosphorylated at several sites and supplies a regulated platform for several partners.
cards.section: Three ways to organize a signal

cards.front: A {{c1::scaffold}} organizes several successive members of one route.
cards.back: Ste5 in yeast is the model.
cards.quote: A scaffold organizes several successive members of one route.
cards.section: Three ways to organize a signal

cards.front: An SH2 domain is a folded module that recognizes {{c1::phosphotyrosine}} and nearby amino acids.
cards.quote: a folded module that recognizes phosphotyrosine and nearby amino acids
cards.section: Three ways to organize a signal

cards.front: Adaptors typically bridge two partners and scaffolds hold several, often three. Why is partner count not the best way to tell the categories apart?
cards.back: Partner count is only a shortcut. The better test is what the protein supplies: a link (adaptor), regulated phosphosites of its own (docking protein), or an organized route (scaffold).
cards.quote: Partner count is only a shortcut: an adaptor typically bridges two partners, and a scaffold holds several, often three.
cards.section: Three ways to organize a signal

cards.front: A receptor phosphorylates many tyrosines on a protein that has no enzyme activity. Different tyrosines recruit different effectors. Is the protein an adaptor, a docking protein or a scaffold?
cards.back: A docking protein. It supplies several regulated phosphosites itself.
cards.why: Holding several partners alone would not identify the role.
cards.quote: A receptor phosphorylates many tyrosines on a non-enzyme protein, and different sites recruit different effectors.
cards.section: Three ways to organize a signal

cards.front: The mammalian protein KSR plays a scaffold-like role. Why is it not a pure scaffold?
cards.back: It is a pseudokinase that changes its partners' shapes and has some kinase activity of its own.
cards.quote: KSR plays a scaffold-like role in mammals, but this pseudokinase changes its partners' shapes and has some kinase activity of its own.
cards.section: Three ways to organize a signal

cards.front: Give the relay that carries a signal from an activated receptor to Ras through an adaptor.
cards.back: Receptor phosphotyrosine → Grb2 → Sos → Ras-GTP.
cards.quote: The first film follows the relay, receptor phosphotyrosine → Grb2 → Sos → Ras-GTP.
cards.section: Grb2 routes a receptor signal to Ras

cards.front: Why does bringing Sos to the plasma membrane help it activate Ras?
cards.back: Ras is anchored to the inner face of the plasma membrane, so bringing Sos to the membrane brings it within reach of Ras.
cards.quote: Ras is a small switch protein anchored to the inner face of the plasma membrane, so bringing Sos to the membrane brings it within reach.
cards.section: Grb2 routes a receptor signal to Ras

cards.front: Which part of Grb2 binds the receptor, and which part binds Sos?
cards.back: The SH2 domain binds a phosphotyrosine on the receptor. The two SH3 domains grip short proline-rich stretches in the tail of Sos.
cards.quote: Grb2's two SH3 domains grip short proline-rich stretches, here the tail of Sos.
cards.section: Grb2 routes a receptor signal to Ras

cards.front: Sos has a second Ras-binding site away from its exchange site. What does Ras-GTP bound there do?
cards.back: It can speed Sos, so each Ras that Sos activates helps it activate more.
cards.quote: Ras-GTP bound there can speed Sos, so each Ras it activates helps it activate more.
cards.section: Grb2 routes a receptor signal to Ras

cards.front: Two receptor tails are phosphorylated equally on tyrosine, but only one has the local amino acid sequence that Grb2's SH2 domain recognizes. Which tail recruits Grb2 and Sos efficiently, and why?
cards.back: Only the matching tail. The phosphate is necessary but not enough; the surrounding residues provide specificity.
cards.quote: The phosphate is necessary for SH2 recognition here; the surrounding residues help provide specificity.
cards.section: Grb2 routes a receptor signal to Ras

cards.front: A mutant Grb2 has intact SH2 domain but both SH3 domains are unable to bind proline-rich stretches. Growth factor activates the receptor. Predict where Grb2 goes and what happens to Ras.
cards.back: Grb2 can still bind the receptor phosphotyrosine, but without SH3 binding it cannot bring Sos to the membrane, so this route to Ras fails.
cards.why: The SH2 domain binds the receptor; the SH3 domains hold the Sos tail.
cards.quote: Grb2's two SH3 domains grip short proline-rich stretches, here the tail of Sos.
cards.section: Grb2 routes a receptor signal to Ras

cards.front: What genetic prediction does a proposed order of a signaling chain make?
cards.back: Switching on a downstream part should bypass a missing upstream link.
cards.quote: A proposed order makes a genetic prediction: switching on a downstream part should bypass a missing upstream link.
cards.section: How experiments found the chain

cards.front: Fly eye cells lacking gene X never become the R7 photoreceptor. Suppose X acted downstream of Ras. What would always-active Ras do in these cells?
cards.back: Nothing: R7 would still fail, because a part after Ras would still be missing.
cards.quote: Nothing: R7 would still fail, because a part after Ras would still be missing.
cards.section: How experiments found the chain

cards.front: In the fly eye, cells lacking gene Z never become R7. Always-active sevenless does not rescue them, and a Ras locked in its GTP-bound state does not rescue them either. Where does Z act relative to Ras?
cards.back: Downstream of Ras, or at least in a step that Ras activation cannot bypass.
cards.why: Rule: a downstream part cannot be bypassed by switching on an upstream one, so no upstream activator rescues a missing downstream link.
cards.quote: A proposed order makes a genetic prediction: switching on a downstream part should bypass a missing upstream link.
cards.section: How experiments found the chain

cards.front: In the fly eye, how did a sensitized screen find genes in the sevenless-to-Ras chain?
cards.back: Simon and Rubin weakened sevenless signaling, then found mutations in fly ras and in Sos.
cards.quote: weakened sevenless signaling, then found mutations in fly ras and in Sos
cards.section: How experiments found the chain

cards.front: Which result with Grb2 and Ras in resting rat fibroblasts supported a role for Grb2 in the pathway?
cards.back: Grb2 plus Ras drove the cells to copy DNA; neither alone did.
cards.quote: found that Grb2 plus Ras, but neither alone, drove resting rat fibroblasts to copy DNA.
cards.section: How experiments found the chain

cards.front: Grb2, fly Drk and worm Sem-5 are orthologs, as are Ras, fly Ras1 and worm let-60. What does this show about the receptor-to-Ras chain?
cards.back: The chain predates the split between those lineages.
cards.quote: Grb2, fly Drk and worm Sem-5 are orthologs, as are Ras, fly Ras1 and worm let-60; the chain predates the split between those lineages.
cards.section: How experiments found the chain

cards.front: In worm, fly and fibroblast, the receptor-to-Ras chain is shared. What differs?
cards.back: What follows Ras: vulval tissue in three of six cells beside the worm gonad, R7 fate in fly cells, and DNA copying in fibroblasts.
cards.quote: What follows Ras differs: three of six cells beside the worm gonad become vulval tissue, fly cells adopt R7 fate and fibroblasts copy DNA.
cards.section: How experiments found the chain

cards.front: How does IRS-1 reach the membrane and the activated insulin receptor?
cards.back: A PH domain binds membrane lipids and a PTB domain recognizes a receptor phosphotyrosine motif.
cards.quote: reaches the membrane through a PH domain that binds membrane lipids and a PTB domain that recognizes a receptor phosphotyrosine motif.
cards.section: IRS-1 turns one input into several branches

cards.front: The insulin receptor phosphorylates many tyrosines on IRS-1. What decides which partner binds at each one?
cards.back: The amino acids beside each phosphotyrosine decide which SH2 protein binds there.
cards.quote: The amino acids beside each phosphotyrosine decide which SH2 protein binds there
cards.section: IRS-1 turns one input into several branches

cards.front: Name two branches that start from IRS-1 after insulin.
cards.back: Grb2 → Sos → Ras, and PI 3-kinase → PDK1 → AKT (AKT helps regulate metabolism).
cards.quote: Two of them: Grb2 → Sos → Ras PI 3-kinase → PDK1 → AKT AKT helps regulate metabolism.
cards.section: IRS-1 turns one input into several branches

cards.front: In cells, every IRS-1 tyrosine that binds PI 3-kinase is replaced by phenylalanine, which cannot be phosphorylated. The tyrosine that binds Grb2 is untouched. After insulin, what happens to AKT activity and to Ras-branch activity?
cards.back: AKT activity falls strongly, while the Ras branch stays close to normal.
cards.why: Different phosphotyrosines recruit different partners, so each branch depends on its own docking sites.
cards.quote: The amino acids beside each phosphotyrosine decide which SH2 protein binds there, so different sites recruit PI 3-kinase, Grb2, the phosphatase Shp-2 and the adaptor Nck
cards.section: IRS-1 turns one input into several branches

cards.front: Cells lack Grb2. Predict Ras activation after an EGF-type receptor signal and after insulin, and what insulin signaling still works.
cards.back: Ras activation through the Grb2 route is lost in both. The PI 3-kinase → PDK1 → AKT branch from IRS-1 uses its own docking sites on IRS-1.
cards.why: Rule: Grb2 sits in two routes that both lead to Ras.
cards.quote: Grb2 now sits in two routes that both lead to Ras.
cards.section: IRS-1 turns one input into several branches

cards.front: In yeast, which kinase ends the mating route, which the filament-growth route, and which the salt-stress cascade?
cards.back: Fus3 ends mating, Kss1 ends filament growth, and Hog1 ends the salt-stress cascade.
cards.quote: The second film traced the shared parts to Kss1 and Hog1
cards.section: Ste5 routes shared kinases

cards.front: Ste11, Ste7 and Fus3 each bind a different region of the non-enzyme protein Ste5. What does this show Ste5 can do?
cards.back: One Ste5 molecule can hold all three kinases at once.
cards.quote: showed that the three kinases bind different regions of the non-enzyme protein Ste5.
cards.section: Ste5 routes shared kinases

cards.front: Why can holding a kinase and its target together increase productive encounters?
cards.back: Otherwise they meet by random drift through a crowded cytoplasm; the scaffold holds both together.
cards.quote: A kinase and its target normally meet by random drift through a crowded cytoplasm, so holding both can increase productive encounters.
cards.section: Ste5 routes shared kinases

cards.front: The first idea was that a dedicated scaffold sequesters its kinase module. What did Wendell Lim's laboratory find does the work in Ste5 instead?
cards.back: Membrane gating and Fus3 unlocking, not locking the kinases away.
cards.quote: Wendell Lim's laboratory later found that Ste5 does not insulate by locking its kinases away; membrane gating and Fus3 unlocking do the work.
cards.section: Ste5 routes shared kinases

cards.front: A yeast cell in high salt has active Ste11 in one salt-stress branch but no pheromone. Why does it not switch on the mating kinase Fus3?
cards.back: Only the mating pathway has Ste5, so only that pathway switches on Fus3; Hog1 also helps keep high salt from activating the mating route.
cards.quote: Restraint also runs the other way: Hog1 helps keep high salt from activating the mating route.
cards.section: Ste5 routes shared kinases

cards.front: Which scaffolds gather proteins in place: one in a fly photoreceptor via PDZ domains, and one at focal adhesions?
cards.back: InaD gathers light-response proteins in a fly photoreceptor; paxillin gathers Ras-pathway proteins at focal adhesions.
cards.quote: InaD uses PDZ domains, modules that grip the last few amino acids of a partner, to gather light-response proteins in a fly photoreceptor.
cards.section: Ste5 routes shared kinases

cards.front: In a model of a scaffolded three-kinase cascade, output rises and then falls as scaffold increases. Why does too much scaffold lower output?
cards.back: The kinases spread across separate scaffolds, so few scaffolds carry all three together. The model calls this combinatorial inhibition.
cards.quote: found that output rose and then fell as scaffold increased, and called the effect combinatorial inhibition.
cards.section: More scaffold can mean less signal

cards.front: In the model, three kinases are each at 100 nM and signaling needs all three on one scaffold. At scaffold levels of 10, 100, 1,000 and 10,000 nM, output is 15, 80, 30 and 4 (arbitrary units). By what factor does output fall from the peak to the highest scaffold level, and what explains it?
cards.back: Peak 80, highest-scaffold output 4: 80 / 4 = 20-fold fall. With scaffold far in excess, the kinases mostly land on different scaffolds.
cards.why: The model assumes fixed kinase amounts; cooperative assembly or other regulation can change the result.
cards.quote: The model assumes fixed kinase amounts and signaling only when all three share one scaffold; cooperative assembly or other regulation can change the result.
cards.section: More scaffold can mean less signal

cards.front: A Ste5 fragment promotes Fus3 autophosphorylation at one of its two activating sites. Must that raise the pathway's final output?
cards.back: No. In the experiment, Fus3 made this way was only partly active and lowered output, so Ste5 tuned the signal rather than just speeding it.
cards.quote: Fus3 made this way was only partly active and lowered pathway output
cards.section: More scaffold can mean less signal

cards.front: Why would a sequence search for relatives of Ste5 in humans miss KSR and JIP-1?
cards.back: They organize cascade kinases comparably but are not descended from Ste5, so sequence similarity would not find them.
cards.quote: KSR in the Ras–MAPK pathway and JIP-1 organize cascade kinases comparably but are not descended from Ste5; sequence similarity to Ste5 would not have found them.
cards.section: More scaffold can mean less signal

cards.front: What do mAKAP hold together, and why does the kinase respond especially to nearby messenger?
cards.back: mAKAP holds protein kinase A and PDE4, which destroys cyclic AMP, so PKA responds to cyclic AMP made nearby before it spreads away.
cards.quote: The kinase therefore responds especially to cyclic AMP made nearby, before it spreads away.
cards.section: Local signals and rewiring

cards.front: A drug blocks PDE4 in muscle cells where PKA is anchored beside PDE4 by mAKAP. Predict the cyclic AMP signal that PKA sees from a brief local burst.
cards.back: The signal can be larger and longer, because local clearance is lost and the messenger may grow and spread.
cards.quote: Its weak point is local clearance: remove the clearing enzyme and the signal can grow and spread.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Why are scaffolds described as rewritable?
cards.back: Swapping one binding surface for another that recognizes a different partner lets an input reach a new output.
cards.quote: swap one surface for another that recognizes a different partner, and an input can reach a new output.
cards.section: Local signals and rewiring

cards.front: What does it mean that scaffolds are rewritable?
cards.back: Swapping a binding surface for one that recognizes a different partner means an input can reach a new output.
cards.why: Rule: separate binding surfaces make scaffolds rewritable.
cards.quote: swap one surface for another that recognizes a different partner, and an input can reach a new output.
cards.section: Local signals and rewiring

cards.front: Two pathways share kinase K. Input A must give only output A, and input B only output B. Design two ways to keep the messages apart, and name each one's weak point.
cards.back: Separate assemblies: scaffold A holds K with A's partners, scaffold B with B's; weak point is dose, since excess scaffold splits partners across incomplete complexes. Separate places: anchor K at two sites, each also holding an enzyme that clears the messenger; weak point is local clearance, since losing the clearing enzyme lets the signal spread.
cards.quote: A good design states what enforces specificity and what failure would break it.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: The mAKAP complex also holds a cardiac target. What is the status of the reports that PKA phosphorylates the ryanodine receptor and that FKBP12.6 leaves?
cards.back: Both findings remain debated; some groups have not reproduced FKBP12.6 loss.
cards.quote: Both findings remain debated, and some groups have not reproduced FKBP12.6 loss.
cards.section: A debated cardiac target
